pair.effect_claim_quote: people often disapprove of experiments involving randomization despite approving of the policies or treatments to be tested.
pair.replication_target_quote: people often rate randomized experiments as less appropriate than the policies they contain even when approving the implementation of either policy untested
pair.outcome_quote: our triangulation reveals insufficient evidence to conclude that people exhibit a common pattern of behavior that would be consistent with relative experiment aversion
pair.review_note: One direct and six conceptual preregistered replications tested generalizability; the source describes failure to generalize rather than universal absence.

pair.original_title: Unskilled and unaware of it: How difficulties in recognizing one's own incompetence lead to inflated self-assessments.
pair.original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
pair.replication_title: Unskilled, unaware, or both? The better-than-average heuristic and statistical regression predict errors in estimates of own performance.
pair.replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
pair.effect_name: Metacognitive deficits explain low-performer overconfidence

pair.replication_target_quote: J. Kruger and D. Dunning (1999) attributed these asymmetric errors to differences in metacognitive skill.
pair.outcome_quote: A replication study showed no evidence for mediation effects for any of several candidate variables.

pair.effect_name: Negative affect and visual memory precision
pair.effect_claim: Negative affect increases the precision of representations stored in visual working memory.
pair.effect_claim_quote: However, in both memory systems, this decrease in capacity was accompanied by an increase in precision.
pair.original_title: Negative affect improves the quality of memories: Trading capacity for precision in sensory and working memory.
pair.replication_title: No evidence that self-rated negative emotion boosts visual working memory precision.
pair.replication_target_quote: Two recent studies (Spachtholz et al., 2014; Xie & Zhang, 2016) reported that self-reported negative emotion boosted the precision with which information was stored in visual working memory.
pair.outcome_quote: six experiments showed substantial evidence against changes in visual working memory precision (and quantity) under negative (and positive) emotion in comparison with neutral, whereas one condition, in one study, showed increased precision under both negative and positive emotion compared with neutral.
pair.replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology Human Perception & Performance
pair.review_note: Six experiments did not reproduce the precision gain, but one condition in one study did; classified mixed.

pair.effect_name: Group Knobe effect
pair.effect_claim: The positive or negative character of a group action’s side effect changes whether people attribute intention to the group.
pair.effect_claim_quote: Building upon this research, we found evidence that the positiveness or negativeness of side-effects of group actions influences people’s willingness to attribute intentions to groups (Experiment 1a)
pair.original_title: “The Group Knobe Effect”: evidence that people intuitively attribute agency and responsibility to groups
pair.replication_title: The Group Knobe Effect revisited: epistemic and doxastic side-effect effects in intuitive judgments concerning group agents
pair.replication_target_quote: In this paper, we investigate the effect described in the literature as the Group Knobe Effect, which is an asymmetry in ascription of intentionality of negative and positive side-effects of an action performed by a group agent.
pair.outcome_quote: We successfully replicate two studies originally conducted by Michael and Szigeti (Philos Explor 22:44–61, 2019), who observed this effect
pair.review_note: The original abstract reports a group intention attribution effect of side effect valence; the later abstract explicitly says its Group Knobe experiments replicated.

pair.effect_name: Averaged music performance preference
pair.effect_claim: A mathematically averaged music performance is rated more highly than most individual performances.

pair.original_title: The Aesthetic Quality of a Quantitatively Average Music Performance: Two Preliminary Experiments
pair.replication_title: Tendency Towards the Average? The Aesthetic Evaluation of a Quantitatively Average Music Performance
pair.replication_target_quote: The present study has investigated the minimal-distance hypothesis in music (Langlois & Roggman, 1990; Repp, 1997) by replicating Repp's original study (1997) on the aesthetic quality of an averaged performance—compared to individual interpretations—of Robert Schumann's Träumerei (Op. 15, No. 7).
pair.outcome_quote: The average performance was rated better than the individual performances, and the lowest rated performance from the original study was rated lowest in this replication as well (large effect size).
pair.review_note: Original average ranked second of eleven, so the claim is higher than most individual performances rather than all.

pair.effect_name: Predatory helpfulness relational shift
pair.effect_claim: Survivors of sex trafficking report a shift from apparently helpful grooming to sexual exploitation.
pair.effect_claim_quote: 17 of the 19 participants were able to identify a distinct relational shift between this grooming stage and the recruitment stage, where CSE began.
pair.original_title: Predatory Helpfulness: An Empirical Framework to Identify Fraudulent Tactics Used by Pimps to Recruit and Commercially Sexually Exploit Young Girls and Women
pair.replication_title: Predatory Helpfulness: A Replication (and Expansion) Study Examining Grooming and Recruitment Tactics in Sex Trafficking
pair.replication_target_quote: Focusing on the fraud and coercion, Basra et al. proposed a new framework, Predatory Helpfulness, which consists of a two-prong process of both a grooming stage priming the victim for seduction, and a recruitment stage which activates the victim into exploitative commercial sex.
pair.outcome_quote: 50 of the 59 participants also spontaneously identified a relational shift that occurred between the grooming and recruitment stages.
pair.review_note: Independent qualitative sample of 59 survivors versus 19 in the original; the relational shift is the paired finding.

pair.effect_name: Parent art therapy group helpfulness
pair.effect_claim: Parents of children with chronic pain find group art therapy helpful and supportive.
pair.effect_claim_quote: Parents enjoyed participating in the group, agreed that they would try art therapy again, and found it to be a helpful, supportive, and validating experience.
pair.original_title: Connecting Parents of Children With Chronic Pain Through Art Therapy
pair.replication_title: Replicating a Therapeutic Art Group Protocol for Parents of Youth With Chronic Pain
pair.replication_target_quote: This study measured the feasibility of implementing a published, parent-only group-based therapeutic art intervention in an IIPT program
pair.outcome_quote: Parents attended 69% of sessions, reported little difficulty attending, and reported a high degree of satisfaction, helpfulness, and support.
pair.replication_journal: The Journal of Child Life Psychosocial Theory and Practice
pair.review_note: The repeated outcome is parent reported satisfaction and helpfulness, not pain relief or a treatment efficacy claim.

pair.effect_name: Unconscious sentence meaning processing
pair.effect_claim: The meaning of masked word sequences is processed without awareness, causing more negative expressions to break into awareness sooner.
pair.effect_claim_quote: the more negative a verbal expression is, the more quickly it becomes conscious
pair.original_title: Reading and doing arithmetic nonconsciously
pair.replication_title: The importance of awareness for understanding language.
pair.replication_target_quote: Sklar et al. (2012) found that sentences, masked from consciousness using the technique of continuous flash suppression (CFS), broke into awareness more rapidly when their meanings were more unusual or more emotionally negative
pair.outcome_quote: we found no evidence that the meaning of a phrase or word could be understood without awareness
pair.original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

pair.effect_name: Context driven Stroop control
pair.effect_claim: Context cues modulate the Stroop effect even for items without frequency bias.
pair.effect_claim_quote: In particular, we demonstrate that context-driven processes can modulate the size of the Stroop effect for frequency-unbiased item types.
pair.original_title: Short article: The flexibility of context-specific control: Evidence for context-driven generalization of item-specific control settings
pair.replication_title: Limits on the generalizability of context-driven control
pair.replication_target_quote: In the current paper, we attempt to replicate and extend one such finding [Crump, M. J. C., & Milliken, B. (2009). The flexibility of context-specific control: Evidence for context-driven generalization of item-specific control settings. The Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 62, 1523-1532].
pair.outcome_quote: Across three experiments we fail to find evidence for context-driven control in the absence of stimulus frequency confounds.

pair.original_title: Why people are reluctant to tempt fate.
pair.original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
pair.replication_title: Magical thinking in predictions of negative events: Evidence for tempting fate but not for a protection effect
pair.effect_name: Tempting-fate actions raise perceived chance of negative outcomes
pair.effect_claim: People judged a negative outcome as more likely after an action perceived as tempting fate.
pair.effect_claim_quote: actions that tempt fate increase the likelihood of negative outcomes.
pair.replication_target_quote: two replications of a tempting fate experiment reported in Risen and Gilovich (2008)
pair.outcome_quote: did replicate the tempting fate effect.
pair.review_note: The separate protection-effect experiments targeted Tykocinski (2008) and failed; that failure does not apply to this original pair.

pair.original_title: Implicit and explicit learning: Individual differences and IQ.
pair.original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology Learning Memory and Cognition
pair.replication_title: COGNITIVE ABILITIES, CHUNK-STRENGTH, AND FREQUENCY EFFECTS IN IMPLICIT ARTIFICIAL GRAMMAR AND INCIDENTAL L2 LEARNING: REPLICATIONS OF REBER, WALKENFELD, AND HERNSTADT (1991) AND KNOWLTON AND SQUIRE (1996) AND THEIR RELEVANCE FOR SLA
pair.effect_name: Explicit learning shows more individual variation than implicit grammar learning
pair.effect_claim: Individual performance varied more in explicit series-completion learning than in implicit artificial-grammar learning.
pair.effect_claim_quote: Substantial individual differences were found between subjects on the explicit task; relatively small individual differences were found on the implicit task.
pair.replication_target_quote: replications of studies of implicit artificial grammar (AG) learning and explicit series-solution learning
pair.outcome_quote: there was significantly greater variance in explicit compared to implicit learning.
pair.review_note: The variance result replicated; the replication found an IQ relation to implicit learning that differed from the original.

pair.original_title: Perceived Parental Acceptance-Rejection and Artistic Preference
pair.replication_title: Perceived Parental Acceptance-Rejection and Artistic Preference: Replication Thirty Years Later
pair.effect_name: Perceived parental acceptance predicts preference for complex art
pair.effect_claim: Adults recalling more parental warmth and acceptance tended to prefer more complex graphic art.
pair.effect_claim_quote: preference for complex works of art is associated with parental warmth and acceptance.
pair.replication_target_quote: The purpose of our study was to replicate Rohner and Frampton’s (1982) work
pair.outcome_quote: perceived maternal acceptance in childhood was associated with a preference for more complex art forms [similar to Rohner and Frampton’s (1982) findings]. However, our participants’ perceived paternal acceptance in childhood had no association with artistic preference.
pair.review_note: Maternal association replicated, paternal association did not; recalled acceptance and art preference are observational.

pair.original_title: The Conceptualisation of Dreams by People with Intellectual Disabilities
pair.original_journal: Journal of Applied Research in Intellectual Disabilities
pair.replication_title: The conceptualisation of dreams by adults with intellectual disabilities: relationship with theory of mind abilities and verbal ability
pair.effect_name: Some adults with intellectual disabilities see dreams as public physical events
pair.effect_claim: A substantial share of adults with intellectual disabilities misunderstood dreams as perceptually public or physical.
pair.effect_claim_quote: 40% of their replies in answer to questions regarding the non‐physical, private nature of dreams were incorrect
pair.replication_target_quote: aim of the current study was to replicate the results found by Stenfert Kroese et al.
pair.outcome_quote: many adults with ID tend to think that dreams take place around them, can be witnessed by others, can be touched and manipulated, can be shared by others
pair.review_note: Replication confirms the qualitative pattern, not the original 40-percent estimate for each question.

pair.original_title: A hard to read font reduces the causality bias
pair.replication_title: Does perceptual disfluency affect the illusion of causality?
pair.effect_name: Hard-to-read fonts reduce illusory causal judgments
pair.effect_claim: Presenting a noncontingent causal-learning task in a hard-to-read font reduced the illusion of causality.
pair.effect_claim_quote: This effect was reduced when the same task was presented in a hard-to-read font.
pair.replication_target_quote: a hard-to-read font led to a decrease in the magnitude of the illusion
pair.outcome_quote: we found no discernible effect of font type on the magnitude of the illusion
pair.review_note: The direct font manipulation was Experiment 2; a separate contrast manipulation was also null but is outside this pair's coded target.

pair.original_title: Perseverance in self-perception and social perception: Biased attributional processes in the debriefing paradigm.
pair.original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
pair.replication_title: Persistence of Impressions of Personal Persuasiveness
pair.effect_name: Discredited performance feedback leaves persistent ability impressions
pair.effect_claim: Initial impressions of a person's ability persisted after the evidence on which they were based was discredited.
pair.effect_claim_quote: Both actors and observers showed substantial perseverance of initial impressions
pair.replication_target_quote: These results replicate previous impression-perseverance findings obtained by Ross, Lepper, and Hubbard (1975)
pair.outcome_quote: initial assessments of their persuasive ability persisted after the evidential value of apparent success or failure upon which these impressions were based was fully discredited.
pair.review_note: Conceptual replication used persuasive ability rather than the original discrimination task and a different discrediting procedure.

pair.original_title: Semantic effects in single-word naming.
pair.original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology Learning Memory and Cognition
pair.replication_title: What exactly interacts with spelling--sound consistency in word naming?
pair.replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology Learning Memory and Cognition
pair.effect_name: Imageability benefits naming low-frequency exception words
pair.effect_claim: Low-frequency exception words with concrete, imageable meanings were named more accurately and quickly than abstract exceptions.
pair.effect_claim_quote: Participants were slower and more error prone when naming exception words with abstract meanings
pair.replication_target_quote: Experiment 4 replicated Experiment 2 of E. Strain, K. E. Patterson, and M. S. Seidenberg's (1995) study
pair.outcome_quote: obtained the same apparent effect of imageability on naming. That effect disappeared when AoA was entered as a covariate.
pair.review_note: Unadjusted pattern replicated, but age-of-acquisition adjustment removed it; the original abstract did not address this covariate.

pair.original_title: Volitional facilitation of difficult intentions: Joint activation of intention memory and positive affect removes Stroop interference.
pair.replication_title: Intention memory and achievement motivation: Volitional facilitation and inhibition as a function of affective contents of need-related stimuli.
pair.replication_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
pair.effect_name: Positive-affect primes reduce Stroop interference
pair.effect_claim: Brief exposure to positive-affect words reduced or removed Stroop interference in difficult-intention tasks.
pair.effect_claim_quote: Removal of Stroop interference was obtained after exposure to words eliciting positive affect.
pair.replication_target_quote: Replicating findings of J. Kuhl and M. Kazén (1999)
pair.outcome_quote: reduction or removal of Stroop interference was achieved after short exposure to primes eliciting positive affect.
pair.review_note: Replication narrowed the effect to achievement-related positive primes across five studies.

pair.original_title: False fame prevented: Avoiding fluency effects without judgmental correction.
pair.original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
pair.replication_title: On the (elusive) role of oral motor-movements in fluency-based memory illusions.
pair.replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology Learning Memory and Cognition
pair.effect_name: Oral-motor interference blocks the false-fame effect
pair.effect_claim: A secondary oral-motor task reduced the false-fame effect from repeated person-name exposure.
pair.effect_claim_quote: blocking such pronunciation simulations through a secondary oral motor task decreased the false-fame effect
pair.replication_target_quote: fluency effects are eliminated if such judgments are made while these muscles are otherwise engaged
pair.outcome_quote: We were also unable to replicate the finding that an oral-motor task blocks the false fame effect (Topolinski & Strack, 2010).
pair.review_note: Replicators compared gum chewing with a manual-motor task; fluency illusions remained.

pair.effect_name: Motor errors disrupt working memory
pair.effect_claim: Making a motor response error while holding information in mind worsens subsequent working-memory performance.
pair.effect_claim_quote: Motor error commission during the delay period consistently reduced accuracy on the WM probe
pair.original_title: Action errors impair active working memory maintenance.
pair.replication_title: Impact of motor error processing on performance on a working memory task: effect of modulating cognitive load in high and low span groups
pair.replication_target_quote: The presented study replicates the ERIAM protocol of Wessel et al. (2022)
pair.outcome_quote: Results show a replication of ERIAM effect in our sample.
pair.review_note: Replication changed the working-memory probe to recall and varied cognitive load. The error-related impairment appeared under load conditions that differed by memory-span group.

pair.effect_name: Switching toward memory has larger attention cost
pair.effect_claim: Switching attention from something seen to something held in memory is slower than switching from memory to perception.
pair.effect_claim_quote: this switch cost was asymmetric, being substantially larger when switching from (external) perception to (internal) memory than the other way around.
pair.original_title: Attentional flexibility is imbalanced: Asymmetric cost for switches between external and internal attention.
pair.original_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology Human Perception & Performance
pair.replication_title: More efficient shielding for internal than external attention? Evidence from asymmetrical switch costs.
pair.replication_journal: Journal of Experimental Psychology Human Perception & Performance
pair.replication_target_quote: The authors observed an asymmetrical switch cost, which was larger when switching toward internal than external material
pair.outcome_quote: After replicating the original asymmetry (Experiment 1)
pair.review_note: The source abstracts compare directional switch costs, not overall speed on internal versus external trials.

pair.effect_name: Survival processing increases directed forgetting
pair.effect_claim: Processing words for survival relevance increases intentional forgetting compared with processing them for moving relevance.
pair.effect_claim_quote: survival encoding brought about greater remembering (after the remember cue) and forgetting (after the forget cue).
pair.original_title: Effects of survival processing on list method directed forgetting
pair.replication_title: Survival processing and directed forgetting: enhanced memory for both to-be-remembered and to-be-forgotten information
pair.replication_target_quote: In Experiment 1, we did not replicate the findings of (Parker, A., Parkin, A., & Dagnall, N. (2021)
pair.outcome_quote: making survival ratings and moving ratings yielded a similar cost of directed forgetting for List 1 items.
pair.review_note: Verdict concerns the relative cost of list-method directed forgetting; the follow-up also tested an item method and found other memory benefits.

pair.effect_name: Regular ordinals precede irregular forms
pair.effect_claim: Dutch-speaking children learn regular ordinal words before irregular ordinal words.
pair.effect_claim_quote: Not only is the tiered pattern absent in regular low ordinals, we also see that it takes time for children to link drie ‘three’ to irregular derde ‘third.’
pair.original_title: Ordinals are not as easy as one, two, three: The acquisition of cardinals and ordinals in Dutch
pair.replication_title: Many systems, one strategy: Acquiring ordinals in Dutch and English
pair.replication_journal: Glossa a journal of general linguistics
pair.replication_target_quote: offer a replication of the core findings in Meyer et al. (2018)
pair.outcome_quote: Dutch-speaking children acquire irregular forms (such as derde ‘third’) after they acquire regular synthetic forms (such as vierde ‘fourth’)
pair.review_note: Replication added English learners; verdict is the Dutch regular-versus-irregular acquisition order.

pair.effect_name: Direct speech activates voice-selective cortex
pair.effect_claim: Silent reading of direct speech activates voice-selective auditory cortex more than reading equivalent indirect speech.
pair.effect_claim_quote: silent reading of direct versus indirect speech engenders differential brain activation in voice-selective areas of the auditory cortex.
pair.original_title: Silent Reading of Direct versus Indirect Speech Activates Voice-selective Areas in the Auditory Cortex
pair.replication_title: Processing Speech and Thoughts during Silent Reading: Direct Reference Effects for Speech by Fictional Characters in Voice-Selective Auditory Cortex and a Theory-of-Mind Network
pair.replication_target_quote: Previous research has shown that direct reference to speech in stories
pair.outcome_quote: Evidence of elevated auditory cortex responses to direct speech over indirect speech was observed, replicating previously reported effects
pair.review_note: Replication used short fictional stories and contrasted direct speech with indirect speech and direct thoughts.

pair.effect_name: Foreign language reduces illusory causality
pair.effect_claim: Using a foreign language reduces mistaken judgments that unrelated events are causally connected.
pair.effect_claim_quote: those performing the task in their foreign language were more accurate in detecting that the two events were causally unrelated.
pair.original_title: Thinking in a Foreign language reduces the causality bias
pair.replication_title: The foreign language effect in the illusion of causality: Evidence of absence
pair.replication_target_quote: We conducted a replication study with a large sample ( N = 220)
pair.outcome_quote: our results did not support the original findings.
pair.review_note: Replication tested the same proposed foreign-language debiasing effect in a larger sample.

pair.effect_name: Expected testing enhances sleep consolidation
pair.effect_claim: Sleep strengthens learned material more when people expect to be tested on it later.
pair.effect_claim_quote: the mere expectancy that a memory will be used in a future test determines whether or not sleep significantly benefits consolidation of this memory.
pair.original_title: Sleep Selectively Enhances Memory Expected to Be of Future Relevance
pair.replication_title: Future-relevant memories are not selectively strengthened during sleep
pair.replication_target_quote: sought to replicate the seminal finding that the memory benefits of sleep are enhanced when people expect a future test [Wilhelm et al., 2011].
pair.outcome_quote: knowledge of an upcoming test had no impact on sleep-associated consolidation in either experiment
pair.review_note: Follow-up observed a general sleep benefit but no additional benefit from expecting a test; verdict is limited to the interaction.

pair.effect_name: Dissociative PTSD subtype
pair.effect_claim: A distinct subgroup of people with PTSD shows especially pronounced dissociative symptoms.
pair.effect_claim_quote: a small but distinctly dissociative subgroup that composed 12% of individuals with a current diagnosis of PTSD.
pair.original_title: A Latent Class Analysis of Dissociation and Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
pair.replication_title: The dissociative post‐traumatic stress disorder ( PTSD ) subtype: A treatment outcome cohort study in veterans with PTSD
pair.replication_target_quote: This study aimed to replicate findings of a dissociative PTSD subtype
pair.outcome_quote: a subsample of severely dissociative veterans was identified
pair.review_note: Original latent analysis produced three classes including a dissociative subtype; follow-up found four classes including a dissociative subtype in treatment-seeking veterans.

pair.effect_name: Childhood trauma and cannabis psychosis interaction
pair.effect_claim: Childhood trauma and cannabis use interact beyond their separate effects to raise psychotic symptom risk.
pair.effect_claim_quote: However, the presence of both childhood trauma and early cannabis use significantly increased the risk for psychotic symptoms beyond the risk posed by either risk factor alone, indicating that there was a greater than additive interaction between childhood trauma and cannabis use.
pair.original_title: Cannabis use and childhood trauma interact additively to increase the risk of psychotic symptoms in adolescence
pair.replication_title: Replication in two independent population-based samples that childhood maltreatment and cannabis use synergistically impact on psychosis risk
pair.replication_target_quote: To replicate and further investigate this issue, prospective data from two independent population-based studies, the Greek National Perinatal Study (n=1636) and The Netherlands Mental Health Survey and Incidence Study (NEMESIS) (n=4842), were analyzed.
pair.outcome_quote: A significant adjusted interaction between childhood maltreatment and later cannabis use was evident in both samples, indicating that the psychosis-inducing effects of cannabis were stronger in individuals exposed to earlier sexual or physical mistreatment [Greek National Perinatal Study: test for interaction F(2, 1627)=4.18, p=0.02; NEMESIS: test for interaction χ2(3)=8.08, p=0.04].
pair.review_note: The later study uses two independent cohorts and tests the trauma by cannabis interaction on psychotic symptoms.

pair.effect_name: Behavioral sunk cost choices
pair.effect_claim: Prior investments of effort or time can lead people to continue a choice despite its sunk cost.
pair.effect_claim_quote: we argue that, through an effort-justification mechanism, people account for the amount of behavioral resources invested when selecting an alternative, in which case they may fall prey to purely behavioral sunk-cost effects. The results of two experiments support this prediction.
pair.original_title: Sunk‐Cost Effects on Purely Behavioral Investments
pair.replication_title: Behavioral Investments in the Short Term Fail to Produce a Sunk Cost Effect
pair.replication_target_quote: In Studies 1 and 2, we attempted to observe whether this effect occurs for short-term behavioral investments.
pair.outcome_quote: In both studies, a reverse, or no sunk cost effect was found.
pair.review_note: The later study tests short term behavioral investments; its primary studies find reverse or no sunk cost effect, while a different hypothetical scenario showed an effect.

pair.effect_name: WAIS Block Design versus Digit Symbol in alcoholism
pair.effect_claim: Alcohol dependent adults score lower on WAIS Block Design than on WAIS Digit Symbol.
pair.effect_claim_quote: A clear asymmetry was found between the tests, the Block Design being poorer than the Digit Symbol.
pair.original_title: AN ASYMMETRY BETWEEN THE WAIS DIGIT SYMBOL AND BLOCK DESIGN SCORES IN ABSTINENT ALCOHOLICS
pair.replication_title: WAIS Digit Symbol and Block Design Scores in Abstinent Alcoholics: A Replication
pair.replication_target_quote: Previous work has indicated that alcoholics perform more poorly on the Finnish WAIS Block Design than on the Digit Symbol. The purpose of the present study was to replicate that result.
pair.outcome_quote: The same kind of asymmetry was found between the tests, scores on the Block Design being poorer than those on Digit Symbol.
pair.review_note: Original and replication abstracts identify the same measured effect and result.

pair.effect_name: Awareness and emotional attentional blink
pair.effect_claim: Masked fearful faces reduce the attentional blink, whereas visible fearful faces increase it, compared with neutral faces.
pair.effect_claim_quote: We found that, in comparison with neutral faces, masked fearful faces significantly decreased the AB magnitude (Experiment 1), whereas unmasked fearful faces significantly increased the AB magnitude (Experiment 2).
pair.original_title: Emotional Modulation of the Attentional Blink Is Awareness-Dependent
pair.replication_title: No Evidence for an Awareness-Dependent Emotional Modulation of the Attentional Blink
pair.replication_target_quote: Pictures of faces with emotional expressions presented before a temporal attention task have been reported to affect temporal attention in an awareness-dependent manner: Awareness of a fearful face was linked to an increased deficit in the temporal attention task, while preventing the face from reaching awareness was linked to a decreased deficit, both relative to neutral faces.
pair.outcome_quote: In both experiments the finding of an awareness-dependent emotional modulation of temporal attention through fearful faces could not be replicated, even when data were pooled across experiments.
pair.review_note: Original and replication abstracts identify the same measured effect and result.

pair.effect_name: Salience network connectivity and self control
pair.effect_claim: Higher salience network interaction scores are associated with better real life self control.
pair.effect_claim_quote: Logistic multilevel regression analysis showed that higher NII scores were associated with increased real-life self-control.
pair.original_title: Functional connectivity in a triple-network saliency model is associated with real-life self-control
pair.replication_title: Salience network resting-state functional connectivity predicts self-controlled decision-making
pair.replication_target_quote: Here, we attempted to replicate this result using data from our own study where 121 participants completed an fMRI self-control task comprising real-life scenarios and data from a second study (N = 79) retrieved from OpenNeuro (dataset ID: ds002643) where participants completed an fMRI food choice task.
pair.outcome_quote: We could not replicate the proposed role of salience network resting-state functional connectivity in self-controlled decision-making in either of those data sets.
pair.review_note: The later studies use task decisions rather than daily self control and report the opposite direction of the original network association.

pair.effect_name: Traumatic brain injury and emotional feedback
pair.effect_claim: Adults with severe traumatic brain injury have weaker subjective responses to posed emotional expressions than controls.
pair.effect_claim_quote: TBI participants were globally less responsive to the effects of body and facial feedback than control participants, F(1,50) = 5.89, p = .02, η(2) = .11.
pair.original_title: Emotional Regulation Impairments Following Severe Traumatic Brain Injury: An Investigation of the Body and Facial Feedback Effects
pair.replication_title: Subjective emotional experience and physiological responsivity to posed emotions in people with traumatic brain injury.
pair.replication_target_quote: We failed to replicate past research that demonstrated an impairment in the feedback effect in people with TBI.
pair.outcome_quote: Participants with TBI did not differ from controls in their subjective ratings in response to posed emotional expressions.
pair.review_note: The comparison is the subjective response to posed emotions; later physiological results are a separate outcome.
pair.original_journal: Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society

pair.effect_name: Numeracy moderation of natural frequency benefit
pair.effect_claim: Natural frequency formats improve Bayesian reasoning mainly among people with high numeracy.
pair.effect_claim_quote: the performance-boosting benefits of the natural frequency presentation occurred primarily for participants who scored high in numeracy

pair.replication_target_quote: This interaction, either that frequencies improve performance only for those of low numeracy or that frequencies work only for those of high numeracy, would suggest that better performance using frequencies could be due to (nonevolutionary) numeracy effects.
pair.outcome_quote: Results from these experiments consistently failed to replicate previous findings of interactions
pair.review_note: The later paper tests several reasoning tasks; the exact paired result is the numeracy by format interaction.

pair.original_title: Resetting capacity limitations revealed by long-lasting elimination of attentional blink through training
pair.original_journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
pair.replication_title: Training-induced Changes in the Dynamics of Attention as Reflected in Pupil Dilation
pair.effect_name: Brief attentional training eliminates the attentional blink

pair.effect_claim_quote: just 1 h of specific attentional training can completely eliminate AB
pair.replication_target_quote: the AB can be eliminated after a 1-hr training with a color-salient T2.
pair.outcome_quote: Behaviorally, we replicated the original training effect with a color-salient T2.

pair.original_title: Performance benefits of depression: Sequential decision making in a healthy sample and a clinically depressed sample.

pair.original_title: Attachment theory in health care: the influence of relationship style on medical students' specialty choice

pair.effect_name: Subjective truth relativism and misinformation receptivity

pair.effect_name: Positive emotions are easier to maintain

pair.effect_name: Social-support cues resist fear learning

pair.replication_title: Social support and fear-inhibition: an examination of underlying neural mechanisms

pair.effect_name: Hierarchical information is memorized faster

pair.effect_name: Negative material impairs associative memory

Negative affect impairs associative memory but not
 
 item memory

pair.effect_name: Left-prefrontal stimulation reduces mind wandering

pair.review_note: Follow-up also manipulated dopamine availability; verdict concerns the stimulation effect on task-unrelated thought.

pair.effect_name: Women respond better to brief heavy-drinking treatment

pair.replication_title: Superior outcome of females over males after brief treatment for the reduction of heavy drinking: replication and report of therapist effects

pair.effect_name: Brightness words constrict pupils

pair.replication_title: Pupil changes to voluntary and involuntary visual imagery: A unified paradigm with implications for aphantasia research
pair.replication_target_quote: processed brightness-related words (involuntary imagery)

pair.effect_name: Head heart pointing and moral choices

pair.effect_name: Low spatial frequencies support stronger holistic face processing

pair.review_note: Cheung et al. directly retested Goffaux and Rossion with a new face-composite sample. Raw same-trial alignment effects were larger for low than high spatial frequencies, reproducing an uncorrected pattern, but response-bias-adjusted congruency effects were comparable. Candidate DOI metadata and abstracts checked against the publisher DOI registration record; later journal is Psychology-primary.

pair.replication_title: Replication of the music preference (MUSIC) model and evaluation of its association with personality and autistic traits
pair.replication_authors: Zhong Jian Chee, Yvonne Leung, Marieke de Vries
pair.effect_name: Music preferences form a five-factor MUSIC structure
pair.effect_claim: Preferences for music excerpts follow a five-factor structure: Mellow, Unpretentious, Sophisticated, Intense, and Contemporary.
pair.effect_claim_quote: The findings from 3 independent studies converged to suggest that there exists a latent 5-factor structure underlying music preferences that is genre free and reflects primarily emotional/affective responses to music.
pair.replication_target_quote: The current study therefore attempted to examine the five-factor MUSIC model and test its association with Big Five personality traits and autistic traits in an online study of Malaysians.
pair.outcome_quote: The original MUSIC model was partially replicated with virtually identical Sophisticated and Intense factors.
pair.review_note: Chee et al. tested the original MUSIC factor structure with 444 Malaysian online participants and 50 musical excerpts. Only the Sophisticated and Intense factors were virtually identical to the original five; the remaining factors did not closely reproduce. This is a partial cross-cultural replication of structure, not the original Big Five personality correlations. No shared authors. The later paper first appeared online in 2023 and in the 2024 journal issue. pair.original_title: The Psychological Consequences of Money
pair.original_authors: Kathleen D. Vohs, Nicole L. Mead, Miranda R. Goode
pair.replication_title: Discrepant Data and Improbable Results: An Examination of Vohs, Mead, and Goode (2006)
pair.replication_authors: Doug Rohrer, Harold Pashler, Christine R. Harris
pair.effect_name: Money reminders increase persistence on a difficult puzzle
pair.effect_claim: Reminding participants of money increases the time they persist on a difficult puzzle before requesting help.
pair.effect_claim_quote: participants who were reminded of money (play money and money prime) worked longer than control participants before requesting help
pair.replication_target_quote: We attempted 2 high-powered direct replications of the first experiment, which found that money-primed subjects worked on a puzzle nearly twice as long as controls before quitting.
pair.outcome_quote: The replication studies showed no evidence of money priming.
pair.review_note: Rohrer, Pashler and Harris conducted two new high-powered direct replications of Vohs, Mead and Goode 2006 Experiment 1. Both found no evidence that money reminders increased puzzle persistence. The original article reported longer persistence in its money conditions (F(2,49)=3.73, p<.04). The two attempts are reported in one later DOI and counted as one article-level pair. No shared authors. pair.original_title: Sex Attribution to Hypothetical Persons Described by Adjective Trait Lists
pair.replication_title: Sex Attribution to Hypothetical Persons Described by an Adjective Trait List: A Replication
pair.effect_name: Male defaults in sex attribution from adjective lists
pair.effect_claim: When students describe hypothetical people from adjective lists, most descriptions are male, even when the lists include feminine traits.
pair.effect_claim_quote: Most of the descriptions were male with the proportion of males decreasing according to the number of female traits included in the adjective list.
pair.replication_target_quote: In the 1969 study most of the figures described, 81%, were male.
pair.outcome_quote: In the repetition of the study 25 years later, 53% of the responses were of female figures, 26% were male figures, and 21% were either male or female.
pair.review_note: Koenig repeated his own adjective-list sex-attribution task with a later new respondent cohort. The original experiment was conducted in 1969 and published in 1972; 81% of descriptions were male. In the 1995 repetition, 53% were female, 26% male, and 21% either. The original author is also the replication author; the later responses are new data. The reversal concerns the overall male default, not every trait-list subgroup. pair.original_title: Perception of Time: Variations in Verbal Content and Delay of Estimation
pair.original_authors: William F. Vitulli, Yvette M. Nemeth
pair.replication_title: A Systematic Replication of Variations in Verbal Content and Delay on Time Estimation and Short-Term Memory
pair.effect_name: Delayed time estimation produces longer judgments
pair.effect_claim: Estimating a passage duration after a delay produces longer duration judgments than immediate estimation.
pair.effect_claim_quote: Among 218 undergraduate volunteers delay of estimation produced significantly longer judgments regardless of the verbal passage
pair.replication_target_quote: Vitulli and Nemeth reported in 2001 that among 218 undergraduate volunteers delay of estimation produced significantly longer judgments of time regardless of the verbal passage
pair.outcome_quote: Yet post hoc tests with nonsense-syllable data removed showed significance between immediate and delayed time estimations consistent with past studies
pair.review_note: Vitulli systematically repeated the 2001 Vitulli/Nemeth task with 112 new volunteers and added nonsense-syllable controls. The immediate-versus-delayed difference was significant in post hoc tests after the nonsense-syllable data were removed, suggesting a boundary condition rather than an unqualified replication across all materials. William Vitulli authored both papers; the later volunteers are new participants.
